common_name: Hamabo Rose of Sharon (Pale Blush Pink Red-Eyed Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Hamabo is a long-cultivated English selection that has held a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit for decades.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Hamabo produces large, single flowers in pale blush-pink heavily veined in a darker rose tone and marked with a deep maroon-red eye, opening from midsummer into early fall on a sturdy, upright shrub. This older English introduction is valued for its soft, understated color combination, which reads as almost silvery-pink from a distance, and for reliable heavy flowering even in average garden soil. Deadhead spent blooms if volunteer seedlings are unwanted, since it is a seed-fertile selection rather than one of the modern sterile triploid types.

common_name: Jeanne d'Arc Rose of Sharon (Double White Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Jeanne d'Arc is a 19th-century French heirloom cultivar still sold today for its full double white blooms.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Jeanne d'Arc opens ruffled, fully double flowers in pure white that sometimes show a faint lavender flush toward the center as they age, blooming from midsummer into fall on a dense, upright shrub. One of the oldest named rose of sharon cultivars still in commerce, it has proven durable and reliably floriferous across generations of cultivation in average garden soil. Because double-flowered older cultivars can set some seed, deadhead spent blooms if volunteer seedlings become a nuisance.

common_name: Lady Stanley Rose of Sharon (Semi-Double Pale Pink Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Lady Stanley is a Victorian-era heirloom cultivar prized for its ruffled, streaked petals.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Lady Stanley bears semi-double, pale blush-white flowers streaked with soft pink and marked at the base with a maroon blotch, giving each ruffled bloom a distinctive marbled look from midsummer into fall. This Victorian-era selection remains in specialty and heirloom nursery trade for its unusually patterned petals, and it performs reliably in average garden soil with the same toughness as other long-cultivated rose of sharon selections. Deadhead spent flowers if self-sown seedlings are not wanted.

common_name: Meehanii Rose of Sharon (Variegated-Leaf Lavender Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Meehanii is grown chiefly for its creamy-margined variegated foliage as much as for its flowers.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new growth. Meehanii is grown primarily for its broad, irregular creamy-white leaf margins, which brighten the shrub's foliage all season and pair with single, lavender-purple, red-eyed flowers that open from midsummer into fall. Because it is less vigorous than green-leaved rose of sharon cultivars, give it a bit more consistent moisture and avoid deep shade, which causes the variegation to fade toward plain green. Prune out any all-green reverted shoots promptly to keep the variegation from being overtaken.

common_name: Monstrosus Rose of Sharon (White Red-Eyed Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Monstrosus is one of the oldest recorded rose of sharon selections, dating to 19th-century European nursery catalogs.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Monstrosus carries large, single, pure white flowers with a wide, dramatic maroon-purple blotch radiating from the center, one of the most strongly contrasting white-and-eye combinations among the older rose of sharon selections, blooming from midsummer into fall. It has remained in cultivation for well over a century thanks to its bold flower pattern and easy, tough constitution in average garden soil. As an older seed-fertile selection it can self-sow, so deadhead if volunteer seedlings are unwanted.

common_name: Coelestis Rose of Sharon (Single Violet-Blue Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Coelestis is a classic older selection valued for its clear violet-blue single flowers.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Coelestis produces single, saucer-shaped flowers in a clear violet-blue with only a faint darker throat, a cooler and more uniformly colored bloom than the bold red-eyed cultivars, opening from midsummer into fall on a vigorous upright shrub. It has been grown in gardens for generations as a dependable, tough performer in average soil, tolerating heat and humidity with ease. Deadhead spent flowers if self-sown seedlings are not wanted, since it is a seed-fertile older selection.

common_name: Ardens Rose of Sharon (Double Lavender-Purple Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Ardens is one of the oldest named rose of sharon cultivars still in commerce and holds a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Ardens bears fully double, ruffled flowers in a rich lavender-purple, appearing more like small rosettes than the typical single hibiscus bloom, opening from midsummer into fall on a dense, upright shrub. Documented in nursery trade since the 19th century, it remains valued for the fullness of its bloom and its long track record of reliable performance in average garden soil. It needs little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning to maintain shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood.

common_name: William R. Smith Rose of Sharon (Pure White Single Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; William R. Smith is a long-popular selection prized for its unmarked, pure white flowers.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. William R. Smith produces large, single, pure white flowers entirely free of a central eye or blotch, a crisper and simpler look than most rose of sharon cultivars, opening from midsummer into fall on a vigorous, upright shrub. Its clean coloring and heavy, dependable bloom have kept it a nursery staple for decades, and it tolerates heat, humidity, and average garden soil with ease. It needs little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning to maintain shape and maximize flowering wood.

common_name: Pink Chiffon Rose of Sharon (Sterile Double-Flowered Pink Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Pink Chiffon is a patented Proven Winners ColorChoice introduction that joins Blue Chiffon, White Chiffon, and Lavender Chiffon in the same anemone-flowered series.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Pink Chiffon opens frilly, semi-double flowers in soft pink with a puffed cluster of petaloid stamens at the center, giving each bloom the same ruffled, anemone-form look as its Chiffon-series siblings, from midsummer into fall on a vigorous, upright shrub. Like Blue Chiffon and White Chiffon it is a sterile selection that sets little to no seed, avoiding the volunteer-seedling problem of older, seed-grown rose of sharon while blooming heavily all season. It needs little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning to maintain shape and maximize flowering wood.

common_name: Lil' Kim Rose of Sharon (Dwarf White Red-Eyed Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Lil' Kim is a compact, patented Proven Winners ColorChoice introduction bred for small-space gardens and container use.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Lil' Kim is a genuine dwarf rose of sharon, reaching only 2 to 3 feet tall and wide compared to the 8-to-12-foot size of standard cultivars, yet it blooms just as heavily, covering itself with single white flowers marked with a red eye from midsummer into fall. Its naturally compact, well-branched habit needs little to no pruning for shape, making it well suited to foundation plantings, small borders, and large containers where full-size rose of sharon would overwhelm the space. It tolerates heat and humidity as readily as its larger relatives.

common_name: Lil' Kim Red Rose of Sharon (Dwarf White Deep Red-Eyed Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Lil' Kim Red is a patented dwarf sibling of Lil' Kim with a noticeably larger, deeper red central eye.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Lil' Kim Red keeps the same compact, 2-to-3-foot dwarf habit as the original Lil' Kim but carries a noticeably larger, more saturated deep red eye against its white petals, creating a bolder, higher-contrast flower on the same small-space-friendly shrub. It blooms heavily from midsummer into fall and needs little to no pruning to maintain its naturally tidy, well-branched form. Like its sibling, it is well suited to foundation plantings, borders, and large containers.

common_name: Lil' Kim Violet Rose of Sharon (Dwarf Violet-Blue Red-Eyed Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Lil' Kim Violet is a patented dwarf sibling of Lil' Kim bred for violet-blue flower color on the same compact frame.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Lil' Kim Violet shares the same tidy 2-to-3-foot dwarf habit as its Lil' Kim siblings but opens single, violet-blue flowers with a small red eye, giving small-space gardeners a cooler color option in the same compact form. It blooms prolifically from midsummer into fall and needs little to no pruning to maintain its naturally well-branched shape. It performs well in foundation plantings, mixed borders, and large containers where full-size rose of sharon cultivars would be too large.

common_name: Totus Albus Rose of Sharon (Pure White Double Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Totus Albus is an older heirloom cultivar prized for flowers that stay entirely unmarked white as they mature.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Totus Albus produces single to semi-double flowers that open pure white and, unlike many other white rose of sharon cultivars, keep no red or maroon eye at any stage of bloom, from midsummer into fall on a vigorous, upright shrub. This older selection has stayed in specialty nursery trade for its unusually clean, unmarked coloring, and it grows and blooms as reliably as other long-cultivated rose of sharon in average garden soil. As a seed-fertile older cultivar it can self-sow, so deadhead spent flowers if volunteer seedlings are unwanted.

common_name: Paeoniflorus Rose of Sharon (Double Rose-Pink Peony-Flowered Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Paeoniflorus is a long-cultivated heirloom selection named for its dense, peony-like double blooms.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Paeoniflorus bears dense, fully double flowers in rose-pink, packed with layered petals that give each bloom the rounded, ruffled look of a small peony rather than the open, saucer-shaped form typical of single rose of sharon cultivars, opening from midsummer into fall. This heirloom selection has remained in cultivation for its unusually full flower form and dependable, heavy bloom in average garden soil. As an older, seed-fertile cultivar it can self-sow, so deadhead spent flowers if volunteer seedlings are unwanted.
